name: Name familiar shapes
description: Student can name familiar two-dimensional shapes such as circle, triangle, square, rectangle and oval.
exampleOfSuccess: Shown a set of shape cards, the student names the circle, triangle, square and rectangle.
commonError: Student calls any four-sided shape a square, or any round shape a circle.
checkpointTask: Show shape cards including a square and a non-square rectangle, and a circle and an oval. Ask the student to name each.

name: Recognise shapes in the environment
description: Student can find and name familiar shapes in objects around them.
exampleOfSuccess: The student points out that a clock is a circle, a window is a rectangle and a slice of toast can be a square.
commonError: Student only recognises shapes on flat cards and does not connect them to real objects.
checkpointTask: Ask the student to find and name three familiar shapes in objects around the room.

name: Make a familiar shape
description: Student can make a familiar shape by drawing, using materials, or combining other shapes.
exampleOfSuccess: The student makes a triangle with three craft sticks, or draws a rectangle.
commonError: Student makes a shape with the wrong number of sides or corners, such as a four-sided 'triangle'.
checkpointTask: Ask the student to make a square and a triangle using sticks or by drawing.

name: Sort shapes by an obvious feature
description: Student can sort a collection of shapes into groups by an obvious feature, such as number of sides or straight versus curved edges.
exampleOfSuccess: The student sorts shapes into 'straight sides' and 'curved sides', putting circles and ovals together.
commonError: Student sorts by colour or size instead of by a shape feature.
checkpointTask: Give a mixed set of shapes. Ask the student to sort them by a shape feature and say their rule.

name: Describe a shape by its features
description: Student can describe a shape by features such as the number of sides and corners, including identifying a shape by feel.
exampleOfSuccess: Feeling a shape hidden in a bag, the student says it has three straight sides and three corners, so it is a triangle.
commonError: Student describes a shape only by what it looks like ('like a roof') rather than by sides and corners.
checkpointTask: Put shapes in a bag. Ask the student to feel one and describe its sides and corners before naming it.

name: Compare two shapes
description: Student can compare two shapes and say how they are the same and how they are different.
exampleOfSuccess: Comparing a square and a rectangle, the student says both have four straight sides and four corners, but the rectangle is longer than it is wide.
commonError: Student lists features of each shape separately without comparing, or notices only differences.
checkpointTask: Give the student two shapes. Ask them to say one way they are the same and one way they are different.

name: Compare objects built from the same blocks
description: Student can compare different objects built from the same number of blocks and describe how they differ.
exampleOfSuccess: Using six blocks each, the student builds a tall tower and a flat row and says they used the same blocks but look different.
commonError: Student thinks the object with more blocks visible from the front has more blocks overall.
checkpointTask: Give the student blocks. Ask them to build two different objects with the same number and compare them.
reviewNotes: From elaboration 3. Introduces 3D object comparison alongside 2D shape work.

name: Follow a single direction
description: Student can follow a single positional or directional instruction, such as forwards, backwards, left or right.
exampleOfSuccess: Told to take two steps forwards, the student does so.
commonError: Student confuses left and right, or moves in a random direction.
checkpointTask: Give the student single movement instructions (forwards, back, left, right). Check they follow each.

name: Describe where something is
description: Student can use positional language such as next to, behind, in front of and between to say where something is.
exampleOfSuccess: The student says the ball is under the table and the bag is next to the door.
commonError: Student uses vague words like 'there' instead of positional language.
checkpointTask: Place objects around the room. Ask the student to describe where each one is.

name: Follow a sequence of directions
description: Student can follow a set of two or more directions in order to reach a location.
exampleOfSuccess: Following 'forwards three, turn left, forwards two', the student arrives at the right spot.
commonError: Student follows the steps out of order, or carries out only the first instruction.
checkpointTask: Give the student a short sequence of directions to a target. Check they follow them in order.

name: Give directions to move someone
description: Student can give clear directions for another person or object to move to a location.
exampleOfSuccess: The student directs a partner 'forwards, forwards, turn right, stop' to reach the door.
commonError: Student gives directions that are unclear or leave out a step, so the partner cannot follow them.
checkpointTask: Ask the student to direct a partner or a toy to a target using their own instructions.

name: Use ordinal and positional language in a line
description: Student can use ordinal language (first, second, third, last) and positional language to place or describe people in a line.
exampleOfSuccess: The student places themselves third in line and says who is first and who is last.
commonError: Student miscounts the position, or confuses ordinal words such as second and third.
checkpointTask: Line up a group. Ask the student to say who is first, third and last, and to stand in a named position.

name: Create and follow an algorithm of moves
description: Student can create a set of step-by-step instructions (an algorithm) to move an object to a target, and follow it.
exampleOfSuccess: The student writes or arranges arrow cards to move a toy through a maze, then follows the steps to check it works.
commonError: Student writes steps that skip a move or point the wrong way, and does not test whether the steps reach the target.
checkpointTask: Give the student a start and a target. Ask them to make a set of move instructions and test that it works.
reviewNotes: From elaboration 2. Algorithm language connects to Digital Technologies but sits within this Maths descriptor.
